---
title: "Word-sized charts, inline in the text"
description: "vsparkline() draws an axis-free chart small enough to sit in a sentence. plot_svg() turns it into inline SVG that inherits the surrounding text colour."
categories: [Text, Statistical]
image: figs/sparkline-shapes.png
---

```{r}
#| include: false
source("_helper.R")

# Turn a sparkline into inline SVG that flows with the text: drop the XML
# prolog, make the backgrounds transparent, and let the default ink follow the
# paragraph's colour (currentColor) so it works in both the light and dark theme.
spark_inline <- function(...) {
  s <- plot_svg(vsparkline(...))
  s <- sub("^<[?]xml[^>]*[?]>\\s*", "", s)
  s <- gsub("fill=\"#ffffff\"", "fill=\"none\"", s)
  s <- gsub("#4d4d4d", "currentColor", s)
  sub("<svg ", "<svg style=\"vertical-align:-0.2em\" ", s)
}

idx <- function(name, n = 60) {
  v <- as.numeric(datasets::EuStockMarkets[, name])
  v[round(seq(1, length(v), length.out = n))]
}
dax  <- spark_inline(idx("DAX"), width = 24, height = 5)
smi  <- spark_inline(idx("SMI"), width = 24, height = 5)
cac  <- spark_inline(idx("CAC"), width = 24, height = 5)
ftse <- spark_inline(idx("FTSE"), width = 24, height = 5)
```

Edward Tufte called a sparkline a "dataword": a chart small enough to sit in a
line of prose, read at a glance, and then move past. Its point is context. A
number in a sentence tells you where a series ended; a sparkline next to it shows
you the whole path that got there, without breaking your reading to look at a
figure somewhere else on the page.

`vsparkline()` draws one. It takes a numeric vector, no axes, and a size in
millimetres, and returns an ordinary plot. `plot_svg()` renders any vellumplot
object to a self-contained SVG string, so a sparkline can go straight into the
running text. Over 1991 to 1998 the German DAX `r dax` and Swiss SMI `r smi`
more than tripled, while the French CAC `r cac` and British FTSE `r ftse` roughly
doubled; all four fell sharply in the last months of the series. Each of those is
a live SVG, sized to the line and coloured to match the paragraph.

The trick that makes it sit in the text is a short helper: strip the XML header,
set the background fills to `none`, and swap the default grey ink for
`currentColor`, so the mark takes the colour of whatever text surrounds it. That
last step is what keeps it legible when the reader flips this site to dark mode.

```{r}
#| eval: false
spark_inline <- function(...) {
  s <- plot_svg(vsparkline(...))
  s <- sub("^<[?]xml[^>]*[?]>\\s*", "", s)           # drop the XML prolog
  s <- gsub("fill=\"#ffffff\"", "fill=\"none\"", s)  # transparent background
  s <- gsub("#4d4d4d", "currentColor", s)            # ink follows text colour
  sub("<svg ", "<svg style=\"vertical-align:-0.2em\" ", s)
}
```

Then drop the result into the prose with an inline R expression. Pandoc treats
the returned `<svg>` as raw HTML and passes it straight through, so the chart
lands mid-sentence with no figure environment around it.

## Three shapes

`vsparkline()` draws three kinds of series. `"line"` traces a trend and marks
the extremes with a dot; `"bar"` is a column micro-chart for counts or volumes;
`"winloss"` reduces a series to equal up and down bars about a baseline, for
streaks of binary outcomes. The figure stacks all three, built from a stock
index, its monthly trading volume, and its daily up-or-down days.

```{r}
i <- as.numeric(datasets::EuStockMarkets[, "DAX"])
line    <- vsparkline(i[round(seq(1, length(i), length.out = 60))], width = 55, height = 12)
bars    <- vsparkline(rpois(28, 6), type = "bar", width = 55, height = 12)
winloss <- vsparkline(sign(diff(i))[1:60], type = "winloss", width = 55, height = 12)

p <- concat(line, bars, winloss, design = "A\nB\nC")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
vg(p, "sparkline-shapes")
```

## A trend callout inside a plot

`annotate("sparkline", ...)` drops a sparkline at a data coordinate, so a chart
can carry a small trend note right where it belongs. The monthly airline
passenger counts below swing wider every year, and the noise makes the trend
hard to read off the points. A sparkline of the yearly totals, floated into the
empty corner, states the trend the detail obscures: steady growth, no wobble.

```{r}
ap <- datasets::AirPassengers
monthly <- data.frame(year = as.numeric(time(ap)), pax = as.numeric(ap))
yearly  <- as.numeric(tapply(ap, floor(time(ap)), sum))

p <- vplot(monthly) |>
  mark_line(x = year, y = pax, color = "grey55") |>
  mark_point(x = year, y = pax, size = 0.8) |>
  annotate("sparkline", x = 1951, y = 580, values = yearly,
           width = 34, height = 11, halign = "left") |>
  labs(title = "Air passengers, 1949 to 1960", x = "year", y = "monthly (thousands)")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
vg(p, "sparkline-callout")
```

For sparklines that live in a table rather than a sentence, see
[sparklines in a table](sparkline-tables.qmd).
